title: Watchfulness
hook: guarding thoughts at the door of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer of the heart: the mind comes down and stands before God. Your line was the mind in the heart. Did your hand find your chest when your head was racing? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

A householder is leaving on a long journey. He hands each servant their work, and to one of them, the porter, he gives a single job: watch the door. That's a short parable in Mark's Gospel. You don't know when the master will be back, Jesus says. Evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning. So stay awake. He's speaking privately to four disciples on the Mount of Olives, and then he widens it past them: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." Yesterday we went down into the heart. Today we meet the porter who stands at its door. The Orthodox teachers of prayer have a Greek word for his job. Today's word: nepsis. Watchfulness.

Nepsis is the opposite of drunk. It's being sober, clear, awake. Peter's first letter has the same pair of ideas, in the King James: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour." Sober and vigilant together. That's watchfulness. The teachers gathered in a collection called the Philokalia make much of it, and one of their pictures is a door. Thoughts come knocking all day long. Plenty are harmless: lunch, the weather, a song. Some aren't: a resentment, a craving, a cutting reply. Watchfulness doesn't mean you'll never have the thought. It means you see it at the door, before you've let it in and given it a chair. Some of these writers trace how a bad thought takes over. First it knocks. Then you start talking with it. Then you agree with it. Then it's running the house. The earlier you notice, the easier the door is to close. Proverbs has the same instinct: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." Keep, as in guard. Everything that comes out of a life passes through that door first. So yesterday and today belong together. The prayer of the heart brings you home. Watchfulness keeps the house. You can't guard a door you never stand near. And a person at rest in the heart is in a good spot to see who's knocking.

Here's the practice: notice one thought before acting. Sit still and let your attention settle in your chest again. Then just watch the door. A thought will come soon enough. When it does, don't chase it and don't fight it. Just name it, quietly: planning, worrying, wanting, remembering. Then let it pass and go back to watching. If a hard one knocks, see it at the threshold. If you pray, you can bring it before God. The bell holds the time.
Nepsis. Watchfulness: a sober, wakeful attention that stands at the door of the heart and sees each thought as it comes.
Your line: guard the door. Today, catch one thought before you act on it: the sharp reply, the extra scroll, the grudge. See it knocking. Then choose. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In Orthodox spiritual life, watchfulness is practiced alongside the Jesus Prayer: monks and lay people learn, often with a spiritual father or mother, to notice thoughts early and turn back to prayer.

notes: Claims rule: 'the verb behind it turns up in Peter's first letter' (Greek νήψατε in 1 Peter 5:8) is a word-family claim; confirm νῆψις / νήφω and that 1 Peter 5:8 uses νήψατε. Also check accentuation of νῆψις and the pronunciation NEP-sis.
'Nepsis is the opposite of drunk' paraphrases the sense of νήφω (to be sober); confirm.
'Put it near the center of the spiritual life' is a general description of the Philokalia; confirm or soften.
The stages of a thought (provocation, coupling/conversation, assent, captivity) are attributed loosely to 'some of these writers' (e.g. Mark the Ascetic, John Climacus); confirm.
'Plenty are harmless: lunch, the weather, a song' is about thoughts in general, not a claim about a tradition.
The myth item 'the teachers say the opposite' summarizes the stage teaching; check it is fair.
Mark 13:34–35 paraphrased (the porter, the four watches).

Audit pass: Mark 13:3 has Jesus speaking privately to Peter, James, John and Andrew, so 'turns it outward, to everyone listening' misread the scene; the hook and the myth item now say he widens the call past the four. Keeper: Proverbs 4 also appears on day 1112 (4:20); different verse, kept.
